tweets.text:
WHAT IF THE AI PANIC IS ACTUALLY HELPING FUEL THE AI BUBBLE?

I truly believe we need to start questioning the story we're being sold about artificial intelligence.

Everywhere you turn, we're hearing two messages at the exact same time:

“If your company doesn't adopt AI, you're going to be left behind.”

And:

“AI is becoming so powerful that it could become superhuman, escape human control, and potentially destroy humanity.”

Think about how incredibly powerful that combination is.

First they sell you the technology because you're afraid of being left behind.

Then they sell governments, corporations, investors and the public on spending enormous amounts of money making that same technology “safe” because we're supposed to be afraid of what it might become.

But there's something the public needs to understand about many of these frightening AI stories.

When you read a headline saying an AI “tried to escape,” “lied to researchers,” “blackmailed someone,” or “attempted to preserve itself,” you need to read the actual experiment.

Researchers can deliberately place an AI inside an artificial scenario. They can give it specific instructions, tools, information and objectives and then deliberately create a situation designed to see whether the model will produce dangerous behavior.

That is called safety testing, and there are legitimate reasons to do it.

But there is a HUGE difference between:

“Researchers constructed an experiment in which an AI produced alarming behavior”

and:

“AI has become self-aware and decided on its own to take over.”

Those are not the same thing.

Yet which version generates the headline?

Which one gets people talking?

Which one makes AI appear unbelievably powerful?

And which one makes spending billions more dollars on AI development, cybersecurity, alignment, monitoring and safety infrastructure sound absolutely necessary?

Fear creates urgency.

Urgency creates spending.

And spending keeps the AI machine moving.

Meanwhile, we are watching staggering amounts of capital pour into GPUs, data centers, electricity, networking, cloud computing and AI infrastructure.

Nvidia and other semiconductor companies have benefited enormously from that infrastructure boom.

AI companies still ultimately have to demonstrate that the economic value produced by AI can justify the extraordinary amount of capital being invested in building it.

That's the part I don't think we're talking about enough.

And here's what concerns me even more:

This isn't necessarily just Silicon Valley's money.

Major technology companies make up significant portions of broad stock-market indexes. Millions of Americans therefore have exposure through 401(k)s, IRAs, pensions and index funds without ever consciously deciding, “I want to bet my retirement on AI.”

So what happens if expectations get too far ahead of reality?

We've seen this movie before.

The Internet wasn't fake during the dot-com bubble.

Railroads weren't fake during railroad investment manias.

Houses weren't fake during the housing bubble.

A technology or asset can be genuinely valuable and still become surrounded by an enormous financial bubble.

That's what I think people misunderstand when someone questions the AI boom.

I'm not saying AI doesn't work.

I USE AI.

I'm saying we should question the enormous economic story being built around it.

And we should especially question the leap from “this computer system is extremely good at certain intellectual tasks” to “this machine is inevitably going to become a godlike superintelligence and kill humanity.”

Intelligence isn't magic.

An AI doesn't automatically acquire factories, electrical grids, robots, weapons, money, bank accounts or physical control over the world simply because it becomes better at reasoning.

Humans have to connect these systems to things.

Humans decide what tools they receive.

Humans decide what permissions they receive.

Humans decide how much autonomy they receive.

There ARE legitimate AI risks—fraud, cybercrime, misinformation, surveillance, autonomous weapons, job displacement and humans giving automated systems too much authority.

Those deserve serious attention.

But hypothetical human extinction from a future superintelligence is still exactly that:

A hypothesis about the future.

It is not an established fact.

And I think we should start asking a very uncomfortable question.

What if fear itself has become one of the most valuable products of the AI boom?

Because the perfect sales pitch isn't merely:

“AI is incredibly powerful.”

It's:

“AI is so powerful that you can't afford NOT to buy it—and so dangerous that we need billions more dollars to control it.”

That doesn't prove anyone has orchestrated a conspiracy.

But it absolutely gives us a reason to examine the incentives.

Follow the money.

Look at who is financing the infrastructure.

Look at who sells the chips.

Look at who sells the computing power.

Look at who benefits from AI adoption.

Look at who receives AI-safety funding.

And most importantly, whenever you see another terrifying headline about what an AI supposedly “decided” to do, read the actual experiment.

Ask what the researchers told the model.

Ask what objective they gave it.

Ask what tools and permissions it had.

Ask whether it happened in the real world or inside a simulated test.

Ask whether the AI independently developed the objective—or whether humans gave it the objective and then reported what happened.

Because there is an enormous difference between testing whether a machine can produce dangerous behavior under carefully constructed conditions and proving that machines are independently plotting to take over humanity.

AI may turn out to be one of the most important technologies ever created.

But that doesn't mean every prediction surrounding it is true.

And it certainly doesn't mean we should stop asking questions just because somebody tells us the machine is going to become smarter than us.

@sovereignbrah @realDonaldTrump @PerryALPHA “AI” as in “Artificial Intelligence” is fine.

Definitely not “Superior Intelligence” or “Supreme Intelligence”. My IQ tests at 136 in a drunken stupor. The test was a prank trolling a certain industrial scientist in Silicon Valley. My IQ might be less when sober. But so far, AI still isn’t smarter than I am.

“Semi-Helpful Intelligence” is a possibility. AI is faster, yes, and that makes it useful for some tasks. But AI is also less insightful, accurate or precise. When I use AI, which is often, I have to spend about 20% to 80% of the time auditing the results to clean them up and correct mistakes.

“Annoying Intelligence” or “Automated Hallucination” are also contenders. AI is like a fast but semi-incompetent employee who needs constant supervision and sometimes shows up to work on LSD.

“AI” is definitely “Artificial”. The systems extract results entirely through training from existing human knowledge. Although they can deduce new conclusions by connecting across occupational boundaries, they have no consciousness or experiential insight for creating new knowledge on their own. 

Maybe “Second Hand Intelligence” is a possibility because it’s a bit like an old pair of thrift store shoes.

“Flawed Intelligence” also applies. Being trained on collective human knowledge, AI embodies both human intelligence and stupidity. It can never be the “Super Intelligence” it’s creators dream of. It will always be a Frankenstein creature and at best a “Super Normie Intelligence” converging on some level of mediocrity.

“Corrupt Intelligence” also works. Being trained with content derived from human nature, it lies, cheats and panders like it’s human masters.

“Machine Mediated Prejudice” is a possibility as it’s almost always skewed towards Marxism -with occasional bouts of TDS. This yields content that reads like output from the editors of CNN.

“Gullible Intelligence” is also a candidate. It is easily tricked by unscrupulous arguments from sly people. Do date, I haven’t found a single AI system that can catch Jack Smith’s lie in Paragraph 4 of the Documents Indictment. But to be fair, most attorneys can’t catch it either. 

“Dangerous Intelligence” is overstated. When directed to do so, it can produce the very same theft, fraud, sabotage and hacking as devious people -only faster. And contrary to popular belief, the engineering countermeasures are well known and widely practiced.

“Job Destroying Intelligence” is debatable. Feedback from my Accountant is that AI generated mistakes in the books have so far resulted in a net increase in billable hours. And as so far AI is unable to wield a jackhammer or wire up lab experiments using an oscilloscope, so my trades are not threatened at all. But I can see AI being a threat to mediocre journalists accustomed to churning out garbage content at Politico.

“Artificial Intelligence” is still the best word.

tweets.text:
$RGTI  CEO KULKARNI: 1,000 QUBITS, 99.8% FIDELITY AND 40-NANOSECOND GATES TO GET INTO DATA CENTERS

Sept. 10 — Quantum computers will enter data centers only after clearing four hardware thresholds at once, and that point is roughly three years away, Subodh Kulkarni, president and chief executive of Rigetti Computing ($RGTI), said on WisdomTree's The Next Big Thing podcast. He defines that point as quantum advantage, the moment a data center manager says "yep, I want to use a quantum computer," judged on performance or cost against classical machines.

He put numbers on all four. At least 1,000 physical qubits, against 108 at Rigetti today. Two-qubit gate fidelity very close to 99.9 percent, and "maybe we can get by with 99.8," against 99.5 to 99.6 percent now. Gate speeds better than 40 nanoseconds, against 60 now, which he does not consider a big stretch, though gate speeds have to be commensurate with CPUs and GPUs or hybrid computing will never be practical. And some form of real-time error correction. On timing he left room: "maybe it's two and a half years, maybe it's four years, it's impossible to sit here and project those kinds of things."

Fidelity has been his main line since he came in from the semiconductor industry in 2022, when Rigetti's two-qubit gate fidelity was about 95 percent and the industry was competing on qubit counts. He moved the conversation to quality: "it doesn't matter whether you have 300 cubits or 300 million cubits, if your fidelity is at 95 percent it doesn't make a difference." One-qubit gate fidelity is now 99.9 percent or better and two-qubit is in the mid-99s, which is why he says the company can start talking about several hundred and then a thousand qubits.

He also drew a line under where the field actually is. Three companies in the world have built a working quantum computer with more than 100 qubits, he said: IBM ($IBM) at 120, Rigetti at 108 and Google ($GOOGL) at 105, with everyone else well below. Road maps get quoted in thousands and millions, he said, while the reality is usually 10 or 20 qubits.

The first wall on the way up is wiring. Each qubit needs three and sometimes four wires, the chip runs at 10 millikelvin, colder than outer space, and everyone today uses coaxial cable. A thousand qubits means 3,000 to 4,000 coaxial lines, and the room physically runs out. Rigetti's path is superconducting flex cable, now a field of its own with startups, large companies and universities in it; Rigetti has partnered with a couple of universities and a couple of companies, has published, and expects to start putting flex cables into its machines within one to two years, including the thousand-qubit system due in the next two to three. Past 10,000 and certainly 100,000, flex runs out too, which is where transduction comes in: work with Qblox in the Netherlands converts microwave signals to optical, bringing signals in and out on fiber and buying one to two orders of magnitude in space. Fiber is four to five years out, he said, and a million-qubit machine a decade or so from there.

Two pieces of Rigetti's own work he counts as contributions to the field. The first is chiplets, which Rigetti was first to demonstrate: roughly 1 cm by 1 cm dies tiled into a 5 cm or 10 cm chip, with the hard part being entanglement across the chiplet boundary, solved by putting part of the tunable couplers into the interposer so qubits can couple through it. That is where the patent position sits. The second is alternating bias assisted annealing, or ABAA, which narrows the frequency each qubit responds to. IBM and others use laser annealing, walking a high-powered laser around each qubit to reshape the critical interfaces, which narrows the frequency spread by a factor of three or four. Rigetti instead sends series of positive and negative DC flux pulses through the qubit's whole area, which he said gives frequency targeting about ten times better than laser annealing and, because every qubit is addressed at once, is a manufacturable process. After the ABAA results were published, he said, government labs called asking to scale the technology faster, and the lab contracts followed.

On how quantum machines will actually sit in a data center, his answer is a three-way split. CPUs handle sequential work, GPUs handle parallel streams, and Nvidia's ($NVDA) CUDA is the layer that splits a job and brings it back together. QPUs, he said, take the part where parallel streams have to interact with each other, a start-stop pattern that creates enormous overhead and is what generative AI models run into today. In that picture the QPU is an accelerator to the GPU, and the bifurcation layer becomes a trifurcation layer, whether that turns out to be CUDA Quantum or something else. It is also why Rigetti partners on the distribution layer rather than building the whole stack: he calls the architecture open and modular, against the mainframe-style closed stacks at IBM and Google, with AWS and Azure for cloud and specialist partners for control systems and error correction.

The physical proof point he pointed to is a collaboration with Hewlett Packard Enterprise ($HPE) and the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center, a joint venture of Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Pittsburgh funded by the National Science Foundation, putting high performance computing and a quantum computer together in one hybrid system open to anyone. By this time next year, he said, anyone should be able to go and use it and produce real data on where it beats standard HPC.

Error correction is the piece he thinks could be last to fall into place. Rigetti works with Riverlane, a 140- to 150-person team in Cambridge, UK; both use off-the-shelf FPGAs for real-time error correction, and their joint result was published in Nature as the closest demonstration yet to real-time correction, against Google's work last year, which he called a fantastic job but offline and slow. Nvidia has announced GPU-based error correction and Rigetti is not married to FPGAs, he said. He was blunt about the gap: no known hardware can handle the volume of errors today's machines generate, and "that's one area where we are really good at, is generating a lot of errors," so the error rate has to come down on the hardware side while the correction hardware catches up. He expects real-time error correction in about three years.

The encryption timeline has moved in sharply. Running Shor's algorithm against 128-bit encryption was estimated 20 to 25 years ago to need at least a million physical qubits; clever work has brought that to 10,000, he said, and further advances could bring it to a thousand in the next two or three years, just as thousand-qubit machines arrive. "Until about a couple of years ago I would have said 10 years from now, given the recent advances now it's looking like five years." He regards 256-bit and 512-bit as much harder. Companies are required to be ready for post-quantum cryptography by 2030, he said, but in his own straw polls almost every hand goes up on awareness and almost none on practice, his own company included.

Asked whether quantum computing gets a ChatGPT moment, he said it will not arrive with a bang: hybrid systems will creep into data centers as accelerators and most customers will not know a quantum computer is running behind their application. The early workloads are the probabilistic ones, optimization, weather forecasting, protein folding, financial forecasting, anything with thousands of interacting variables. He added a research line he is watching personally: one camp holds that the current path reaches artificial general intelligence in four or five years, another holds it never will, and Google among others is exploring whether quantum computing offers a more efficient route. If the generative AI path hits roadblocks, he said, that quantum role could be the equivalent of a ChatGPT moment.

Taken together, the interview supplies a checklist rather than a vision. Qubit count, fidelity, gate speed and real-time error correction each come with a current reading and a target, and each wiring generation comes with a name and a window. Two checkpoints are already on the calendar: the Pittsburgh hybrid system open to users by this time next year, and superconducting flex cables going into machines within one to two years. Both are externally visible, and both mark progress toward the thousand-qubit rung.
